narrative:
A cold front stretches from Pennsylvania across the Appalachians to north Georgia this morning. It slowly drifts east into the Foothills today. We have partial sunshine today, and with daytime heating, scattered mostly afternoon showers and thunderstorms pop up. A shower or thunderstorm remains possible into this evening. A southeasterly flow develops around weak low pressure that will be in north Georgia later tonight. Showers and thunderstorms are around Tuesday as well, but more focused on the east side of the Appalachians. Temperatures are a bit cooler Tuesday, too.

Southern Appalachians – SW Virginia & Western North Carolina

August looks like an ordinary month in an extraordinary summer. While Texas and the southern Plains bake under a stubborn ridge, the mountains sit off to the side and finish close to normal — a shade warm overall, a wet first week, and a drier stretch in the middle.

The Typical August: Just Past the Peak

July owns the hottest days of the year, but August gives up little ground — average highs in August run less than 2 degrees cooler than July’s. The retreat is uneven: Hickory sheds 1.7 degrees for its average high in August while Banner Elk gives up only 0.6 degrees, because high elevations cool slowly in late summer. The real break waits until September, which drops five to six degrees below August. This is the last full month of summer, not the first hint of fall.

August is also one of the three wettest months across the mountains, and at Marion, Morganton and North Wilkesboro it is the wettest of all. The reason is the one that makes July wet: by midsummer the fronts that organize our weather have retreated, leaving the terrain in charge. Daytime heating warms the high terrain faster than the free air around it, lifting moist air until it condenses, and afternoon thundershowers repeat day after day. August highs run from 86 degrees at Lenoir down to 66 on Mt Mitchell, a twenty-degree spread within about an hour-and-a-half drive, with lots of climbing!

The Big Picture for August 2026

The dominant feature this month sits a long way from here: a large area of high pressure stretching from the SW U.S. to the Southern Plains — hot, dry, and stubborn. We are east of the heart of the hot air. The heat anomalies will taper as one goes east toward the North Carolina Mountains.

Meanwhile, at least two troughs slide by to our north and northeast during August — one across the Ohio Valley in the first days of the month, another over the Great Lakes near mid-month. Each turns our winds northwesterly for a few days, which in these mountains means somewhat cooler and drier air. Through the first half of the month, the Bermuda High stays mostly offshore, unusual for August and part of why this month will not be a scorcher overall.

The pattern aloft is generally flat all month — no deep trough, no strong ridge in the eastern United States. We sit in the slack middle, between the heat in the Rockies, heat in the Atlantic, and the cooler north. Neither heat nor cool reaches us with much force.

Temperatures: A Cool Start, a Warmer Finish

The month opens cool. A front approaches from the northwest in the first few days, holding temperatures down with clouds and rain. Behind it, high pressure builds over ground wet since mid-July, and damp soil heats slowly — sunshine evaporates water instead of warming air. This may be the only week of the month with below average temperatures.

The second week turns warmer as the western ridge expands east, though the heat arrives much diminished. Near mid-month a trough settles over the Great Lakes, returning us to northwest flow and knocking temperatures back to normal. That cooling is modest. Nothing truly cool exists anywhere in North America in August, so it means lower humidity and a couple of pleasant mornings, not relief. Wytheville, Galax and Sparta feel it most; Asheville and Hendersonville barely at all.

The last ten days warm again as the Bermuda High finally builds westward into the Southeast, putting the month slightly above average — the Foothills more so than the mountains.

Precipitation: A Wet Start, Then a Drier Middle

The front in the first few days may bring the month’s only widespread organized rainfall. After it fades, high pressure and wet ground take over and afternoon thundershowers fire over the terrain day after day — enough for an above average first week. The second week is less wet and warmer in a southwest flow. The third week is driest, as northwest flow behind the mid-month trough brings sinking, drying air and thins thundershower coverage. The last ten days return to near normal, the rain favoring higher terrain.

The surplus is concentrated in the mountains — Celo, Burnsville and Beech Mountain ten to twenty-five percent above normal, Lenoir and Morganton nearer average. Early-month frontal rain falls fairly evenly; the rest depends on afternoon thundershowers, which favor elevation. Because so much of August’s rain is hit-and-miss, two locations a few miles apart can finish an inch and a half apart.

One thing works against a wetter forecast. El Niño is already inhibiting the Atlantic tropical season, its high-altitude winds tearing storms apart before they organize. In an average August the remains of a tropical system can deliver a big total in a hurry — that door looks closed.

Other Items of Note
  • The models agree more closely on temperature than they usually do at this range — European, American and Canadian ensembles all put the mountains within a degree of normal. They agree less on rainfall, specifically on how far west the wet axis sets up. We sit on that boundary, and small shifts in it matter a great deal to the Foothills.
  • As always, this forecast is built from scratch. We work from large-scale model guidance and climate indices (MJO, NAO, AO, and PNA). From that analysis, we reach our own conclusions before looking at anyone else’s forecast. Most of the large-scale indicators in the summer are either non-factors or weak signals. We relied heavily on a blend of long-range models in this forecast. We check the NOAA Climate Prediction Center outlook afterward, for comparison only, never as an input. The NOAA forecast is a little warmer and drier than our forecast.

The Ocean: El Niño Builds Toward Winter

El Niño is firmly established and strengthening. The warmest water sits in the eastern Pacific near the coast of South America, about three degrees Celsius above normal, tapering westward to near normal at the International Date Line. That geography matters: events with the warmth concentrated toward the eastern Pacific produce the textbook winter response over North America, and this one is about as east-focused as they come. The two graphs below show the current Sea Surface Temperature Anomalies globally and the forecast for the strength of the El Niño in the coming months.

The atmosphere is catching up with the ocean now, which is the sign forecasters look for. Thunderstorm activity that normally sits over Indonesia has shifted thousands of miles east into the central Pacific, and the winds aloft have reorganized to match. That coupling is what lets a warm patch of tropical ocean rearrange weather over North America months later. This will be a very strong El Niño. It peaks in late autumn, holds through early winter, and slowly fades early next year.

Look also at the cooler than average water in the Gulf of Guinea, off West Africa — sometimes called an Atlantic Niña. We flagged it last month, and it has deepened rather than faded. Along with El Niño’s high-altitude winds, it is one more factor working against Atlantic tropical development this season.

The other ocean story is broader: most of the world’s oceans are running warm. The subtropical North Atlantic set record temperatures four months running this spring, and by June roughly eighty-two percent of the global ocean was in a marine heatwave — the second largest extent ever measured. Warmer water puts more moisture into the air, and for us that shows up first in overnight lows. Cool nights are this region’s signature — Jefferson averages a low of 57 in August, Mt Mitchell 51 — and they depend on air dry enough to radiate heat away after sunset. Higher humidity results in warmer low temperatures and means heavier downpours when storms do form.

What would that mean for winter? If this El Niño behaves the way most of them do, the Southern Appalachians finish wetter than normal, with the storm track running along the Gulf Coast and up the East Coast and delivering more systems than an average winter. The record of El Niño winters going back to 1950 shows above-average snowfall across the southern Appalachians.

The catch is that these are typically not very cold winters. What produces the snow is storm frequency and elevation rather than deep cold — the same system that gives Banner Elk and Beech Mountain a foot can give Hickory a cold rain. (This does NOT mean that the Foothills will be without snow or ice this winter.) Expect a busy winter in the Southern Appalachians — with a variety of precipitation types.

We will have much more to say about all of this in the RaysWeather.com Fearless Forecast for Winter 2026/27 that is published in the 3rd week of October.
